headline: A 2015 law extends a federal hiring preference, previously limited to mothers, to certain fathers of fallen or disabled veterans.
what_it_does: The law adds fathers to the group of parents who receive a preference for federal jobs because of a child's military service. Before this law, only mothers qualified. A father qualifies if his child died under honorable conditions while serving in a war, in a campaign or expedition with an authorized campaign badge, or between April 28, 1952 and July 1, 1955, or if his child was a service-connected, permanently and totally disabled veteran. The father must also meet one condition: his spouse is totally and permanently disabled, or he is unmarried or legally separated from his spouse when he claims the preference.

who_it_affects.how: Fathers who lost a child under the covered service conditions can now claim the federal employment preference that mothers already had, if they meet the marital or spousal conditions.
Fathers of service-connected, permanently and totally disabled veterans can claim the preference if they meet the same marital or spousal conditions.
Agencies must apply the expanded preference when they evaluate eligible parents who apply for federal jobs.
Applicants competing for federal positions may face eligible fathers who now hold this preference.

when_it_takes_effect: The summary gives no separate start date, so the law applies from its enactment on October 7, 2015.
